However, the objects of contemplation do not transcend the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and these three natures are themselves the three truths (*trisatya*).

Since the three truths are a single dharma and do not exist as separate entities, the objects of contemplation—being the three truths as one dharma—correspond to the wisdom of contemplation, which is the three contemplations within a single mind (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*).
A single thought-moment fully encompasses all, for subject and object are non-dual;

through this wondrous practice, when contrasted with the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) that correctly expound the Mahāyāna, it is identical to the *Lotus Sūtra* as the primary school of the Tiantai tradition, and its doctrine and principle are in profound accord with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the primary school of the Huayan tradition—both are equally ultimate.
This [distinction] is made by classifying the depth and shallowness of various schools according to their provisional teachings (*upāya*). All these schools...

However, while clinging to [such views] leads to falling into heterodox discourse—where nothing is impossible—how could one possibly equate the ultimate treatise of "consciousness-only without external objects" with the heterodox arguments of the non-Buddhists who claim that primordial darkness (*āṇḍa*) gives rise to consciousness? They cannot be spoken of on the same day.
Answer: In our school’s *Vijñaptimātra*, from the initial resolve up to the ultimate stage of the Sage, in every stage one knows non-existence, which is the contemplation of the True;
in every stage one knows existence, which is the contemplation of the Conventional. Yet, because the conventional does not depart from the True, it is eternally non-existent;

because the True does not depart from the conventional, it is eternally existent. However, this existence and non-existence are but a single essence. How could this be the same as the "non-existence" imagined by those who cling to self-nature? Therefore, it is Great.

The Master said: "If one examines their dual movement, they ultimately return to the wondrous enlightenment of the eternally abiding samādhi. In beholding the various Buddha-lands, they do not do so through dualistic marks;
how could it be that the ultimate state is simply the total absence of objects? How could this possibly be compared to the primordial state of external non-being?"

The answer is: To say that "only consciousness exists and no objects exist" means that consciousness pervades all objects. How could this be the same as the heterodox attachments of the non-Buddhists or the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) calculations?
For even those [schools] who still maintain the existence of a self and dharmas are superior to the non-Buddhists; how much more so when one eliminates even the notion of "only consciousness"?
Vinaya School Questions and Answers, Part Two.
Questioned by Dharma Master Raishō of Japan.
The Response of Dharma Master Rui of Gokuraku-ji to the First Inquiry Regarding the Five Meanings of the Fundamental School’s “Partial Pervasion” (Funtsū) has five parts.

The first inquiry concerns the statement that Trapuṣa was weary of the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*): "This refers only to being weary of the bondage of the fruit and the physical basis, not to being weary of [the path itself]."
Regarding the truth realized in the fundamental Vinaya, it merely states that "this body is not solid," but does not speak of "disgust for the outflow-free.

If that were so, which of all the Arhats would not feel disgust toward the resultant body that binds them? Or could this perhaps refer to the Arhat’s maintenance of the life-force (*āyuṣka-saṃskāra*) as taught in the Abhidharma?
If so, what is the purpose of employing this as a "partially common" (*p’unt’ong*) meaning?

Answer: Regarding the body that serves as the basis for the bonds of the fruit of revulsion experienced by Dharmatāpa—if he had been weary of the fruit itself, he would have swiftly entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Precisely because the Venerable One’s revulsion toward *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* was not a firm disposition, he subsequently cultivated the five meritorious deeds and practiced the Mahāyāna path;
is this not indeed the meaning of "partial penetration" (*fen-tong*)?
Next, regarding the doubt as to whether giving generates the path to Buddhahood—this is the phrase for the dedication of merit by the patriarch of the school.
If this meaning is taken as universal, it should also apply to the Vinaya of the Sarvāstivāda school. Why? Because the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the Sarvāstivāda Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states:
"May the merit [of this] cause all sentient beings together to attain the path to Buddhahood."
Answer: The Sarvāstivāda school has meanings that accord with the Mahāyāna; among these, there are also those explained by the Sarvāstivādins alone.

Although the meditative objects (*vipaśyanā-dharma*) they perceive belong to the specific perspective of the Hīnayāna, because they also possess meanings that accord with the Mahāyāna, they are all classified as Hīnayāna based on the meditative objects they specifically calculate.
Thus, they are designated simply as Hīnayāna.
The three doubts are summoned together under the title "Buddha-sons" (*buddhaputra*). Regarding the name "Buddha-son," there are both general and specific meanings.
Generally speaking, among the disciples of the Three Vehicles, there are none who are not born from the Buddha; thus, in all the Vinayas, they are collectively referred to as "Sons of Śākya.
However, when discussed specifically, the Two Vehicles lack the principle of continuing the lineage of the Buddhas; therefore, the name "Buddha-son" is restricted [to the Mahāyāna].
Therefore, when the term "Son of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra) appears in the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*, it should be understood merely as a general designation.

Response: A general designation refers only to the name for a Śākya-son; however, the term "Son of the Buddha" [specifically] refers to those of the Two Vehicles in the context of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is only upon receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that one first knows for oneself that one is a son of the Buddha;

now, since this very assembly summons you as a son of the Buddha, you know that you are indeed a son of the Buddha and shall attain Buddhahood—is this not the meaning of "partial penetration" (*fen-tong*)? How could it be appropriate to indiscriminately equate this with being a "disciple of the Śākya" (*śākyaputra*) in a general sense?

Regarding the fourth point, the doubt concerning the relinquishment of wealth for communal use is not a grave matter; why then do you claim this is a sectarian tenet? How does it relate to the universal meaning (*arthasāmānya*)?

For example, in the case of pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), one’s own school permits its use to support those of lesser faculties, while other schools prohibit it, which is identical to the Mahāyāna approach.
Nevertheless, this does not mean the meaning is universally applicable to the Mahāyāna; moreover, once the wealth has been relinquished, what offense is there in the Saṃgha using it? And yet...
Kātyāyanīputra, you should know that this is the expedient means of the Hīnayāna. If one relies on the Great Mind, can one not dwell directly within the four seas?

Answer: The relinquishing of wealth and resources is not what is emphasized here; it is merely according to the calculations of this same school. However, they calculate it as being like the empty penetration of a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.

Because there is no sense of attachment, this is the meaning of "partial application" (*prasaṅga*). If one were to commit an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*) by returning the relinquished property, it would be as if the Saṃgha had newly acquired it;

since the property was returned, there would be the benefit of sustaining the body and furthering the Path. However, in the present case, since it is not returned, one merely incurs an offense of wrong-doing against the Buddha’s precepts.
As for the relinquishment of the relinquished property, it is precisely like the Bodhisattva’s mind: empty, pervasive, and without attachment. What offense could there be?
If this [view] is not in accord with the general principle (*sāmānya-pravṛtti*), what does it mean?
Fifth, regarding the doubt that objects are not perceived by the sense organs: it is said that this is also the tenet of a limited school (*hīnayāna-pakṣa*) and not the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
According to that Dharma-lakṣaṇa Mahāyāna, because the nine conditions—including the sense organs, objects, and consciousness—conjoin, the eye is able to see forms, and so forth.
Since the mind and dharmas follow this principle, Jingxi [Zhiyi] set forth the meaning of the Mahāyāna to refute the divergent views of the Hīnayāna, as seen in his *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary).
If that is so, why did the Patriarch [Huisi] take the calculations of the various Hīnayāna schools and define them as being "comprehensive"?

Answer: Because it is dull, the mind does not see form; this is called "not understanding the ultimate meaning. Although there is a conjunction of the four [elements], the mind is the primary factor, and thus it is able to see form.
This is the definitive (nītārtha) tenet of the Mahāyāna school. As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Chapter 30) states:

"There is form, there is light, there is the mind, and there is the eye; because these four are in conjunction, it is called 'seeing. Now, our own school [holds that] it is by means of consciousness...

Since seeing form is identical to nirvana, it is called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Now that one recognizes that the capacity to see form is not something other than the Great [Vehicle], what further doubt could there be?
Second, regarding the increase of the precepts:

when receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, does one who has already received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* according to the Nanshan tradition—thereby giving rise to the perfect substance [of the precepts]—receive the Bodhisattva precepts again?

If it were said that one must receive the complete essence of the precepts through a further formal act, then since the three aggregates would already be possessed, what would be the purpose of receiving them again?

Therefore, we know from the tradition that the patriarchs did not personally undergo the experience of augmenting the Bodhisattva precepts, because the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) itself gives rise to the complete essence;
thus, there is no need for a further reception. Moreover, while the Tathāgata was in the world, the various śrāvakas and others were permitted to reveal and manifest [this truth].
Thereafter, it does not say that one further receives the Bodhisattva precepts;

yet if it says one does not receive them, then since the Nanshan school relies on the *Śīla-sūtra*, which takes the fifty rules of the full ordination as the preliminary means (*upāya*) for a Bodhisattva—just as that sūtra uses the analogy of a four-story pavilion—if one does not receive [the Bodhisattva precepts], then one level of that structure would be missing.
That sūtra states: "If one is to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, one must first generate the mind of the Mahāyāna."
Furthermore, if one has received the *upāsaka* precepts up to the *bhikṣu* precepts, it is impossible that they have not received the Bodhisattva precepts.
Moreover, the *Ye shu* (Commentary on Karma) states: "If one previously did not take the object of compassion as a condition, how could the Great [Vehicle] be contained?

This does it not mean that one receives the Great [Vehicle] later? If one were to say, "Since the essence of the Perfect [Vehicle] has already been generated, one receives the Great [Vehicle] again," [that would be incorrect].
"Indeed, once these words have been uttered, their perfect essence has already been manifested; therefore, they can no longer be received.
Likewise, the Bhikṣu precepts cannot be received, because the Five Precepts and the Śrāmaṇera precepts have already manifested their perfect essence.
If you resolve this difficulty by saying that the Five Precepts and the Śrāmaṇera precepts do not yet fully possess the deportment of a Bhikṣu..."
Since a bhikṣu who must ascend the altar has likewise not yet fulfilled the formal requirements of a bodhisattva, must he necessarily receive it through Mahāyāna ritual procedures?

This question has been subject to divergent views since ancient times, none of which appear entirely satisfactory; I now pose the inquiry once more and pray that you will provide a definitive resolution.
Please do not dismiss this matter, but examine it further in detail for a clear judgment.
In response: although one has aroused the vow of the perfect essence (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it is as yet not perfected, one must receive [the precepts] according to the *Śīla-sūtra*.

As for the claim that one does not see the Patriarchs [in the transmission of] the Bodhisattva Precepts—how could the Patriarchs not be internally manifesting the perfect cultivation of the Bodhisattvas? Why would they necessarily [be absent]?

Regarding the statement that one "receives" [the precepts], it is further said that after the revelation and clarification for the śrāvakas, there is no mention of receiving the bodhisattva precepts again;
for since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, "The path you practice is the bodhisattva path," what need is there to receive them again?

Regarding the third doubt concerning the *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal motion with four proclamations) for the arousal of the perfect body (*pariniṣpanna-śarīra*), I have previously sought instruction on this matter from the masters of the Chan school in the Zhejiang region.

Some have said that once aroused, one must undergo further increase; others have said that if it is aroused, there is no need for further increase, even though such increase exists—it is simply not augmented.
Although these views differ regarding whether the arousal of the perfect [body] is the same as or different from the increase, despite having heard these words, the meaning remains unclear to me now.
I have posed ten difficulties, each striking at the gateway of the doctrine;

this was not done out of a desire to create doubt or engage in frivolous debate, but solely because I wished to personally master its meaning and thereby block [misunderstandings] from other quarters.
Initially, there was confusion and conflation between the Great and Small Vehicles, which is difficult to justify.

It is said that the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure of four announcements) upon ascending the platform belongs to the Hīnayāna teachings, whereas the *tri-saṃvara-karman* (the ritual for the threefold restraint) belongs to the Mahāyāna teachings; how then can these distinct vehicles of doctrine be conflated?

If one argues that by generating the great resolve (*mahācitta*), one attains the Great Vehicle even through the Small Vehicle, why would this be restricted solely to the Dharmaguptaka school? This would also apply if one were to rely on the Sarvāstivāda.

If one claims that generating the mind of the Perfect [Vehicle] (Yuanxin) should also mean generating the precept-substance (jie-ti) of the Perfect School (Yuanzong), then when the Dharmaguptaka school receives the Dharma, it would either generate the Perfect precepts,

or the Sarvāstivāda and the *Dharmaguptaka* schools would likewise do so according to the Emptiness School (Kongzong). To argue that one may simply rely on the generation of the mind without necessarily relying on the formal ritual (fa)—
is such a formulation not a perversion of the essential core of the schools, resulting in a confused conflation of the Great and Small Vehicles?
Answer: Although the essence [of the precepts] is perfected, the reception of the Dharma remains partial; how could there be any confusion between them?
The two masters raise a difficulty based on the contradiction of conditions, saying: "The essence of the precepts in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) originally arises before a single person present;
how could it possibly arise before ten masters on the altar? Indeed, the method for receiving the precepts is the same for both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
If one receives the precepts according to the Dharma, they will be attained; if there is a violation, the precepts will certainly not arise.

Regarding the selection of a master for Mahāyāna precepts, it is said that one must possess the four abilities, five virtues, and be free from the six defects; if even one of these is lacking, one is unfit to be a master.
Now, what grounds do you have to act as a master and arbitrarily establish an altar to transmit the essence of the Perfect Teaching?

Answer: The Patriarch employed the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to open and resolve [the doubts of] those who knew that both the Great and Small Vehicles are mental objects and conditions; he determined that it is only the mind that acts.
This was intended to dispel the dharma-attachments of the Western lands and to cause the multitude with deluded attachments in the Eastern Continent to fall silent.

Whether form-and-mind or non-form-and-mind, there is nothing that is not the substance of the mind. Since the mind is wondrous, it gives rise to the perfect substance. As the Master was about to establish this, he took the distinctions of conditions as his basis.

How difficult this is! If one asks, "Who does not know the distinctions regarding the conditions for a preceptor?"—the third question concerns the contradiction between the prohibitions and the difficulties.
Regarding the difficulty: in the Mahāyāna, one first requests the Upādhyāya and Ācārya—the two masters—and they inquire whether there are the seven *pārājika* (obstructions);
if these seven obstructions are present, the candidate is not permitted to receive the precepts before them. In the Hīnayāna, however, they only inquire about the five [obstructions].
If one does not inquire about the two types of heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), and thus the inquiry regarding the obstacles (*antarāya*) is incomplete, how can the precepts be conferred?
Answer: The essence of what is conferred is precisely the perfect essence; this accords with the Buddha’s own words—how could it have anything to do with the matters of obstacles and difficulties?
Regarding the objection that the four periods of vows are contradictory:

[the opponent] says, "If the *bai-si* (formal act) is for the duration of one's life, yet the fundamental principle is for the sake of the future limit—if one proclaims 'for the duration of my life' with the mouth while intending 'until the end of the future' in the mind, would this not be equivalent to the offense of false speech?
If this is so, can both not be attained?"

Answer: In the *Jieshu* (Explanatory Notes on the Precepts), the Great Master himself poses the question and provides the answer, making the meaning very clear. Furthermore, regarding the offense of falsehood:
for instance, when Queen Śrīmālā pointed to the *Vinaya* as being the Mahāyāna training, it is possible that she had not yet heard of our Buddha’s formulation of the offense of falsehood.

The fifth is the objection regarding the contradiction with ritual procedures (*vidhi*). The objection states: "The ritual procedures for receiving the precepts differ between the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna;
the Mahāyāna relies on the Mahāyāna, and the Hīnayāna relies on the Hīnayāna. How could one recklessly employ [the other]?

Even if there are differences within the Hīnayāna itself, they are not indiscriminately applied—just as one adds specific robes or adopts the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* instead of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. How much more so, then, regarding the Mahāyāna ordination?
If one does not employ the threefold *karmavācanā* for the precepts but instead uses the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle to develop the perfect essence,
how could it be possible— just as it is for a low-ranking official— to attain the rank of a great minister?

Answer: To now claim that the perfect nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is produced by the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion consisting of one proclamation and three announcements) is precisely like a low-ranking official hoping for a high position.
Since you already understand this point, why do you still harbor doubts?

Sixth, the objection concerning the production of the nature: It is asked, "When it is said that the perfect nature is produced, does it mean that the formal body (*rūpa*) and the mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*) are produced simultaneously?"

Regarding the statement that "the stages are identical," if one says they are identical, one should now ask in return: does this identity refer to the stage of principle (*li-ji*) or the stage of phenomena (*shi-ji*)?
If one says it is the stage of principle, this meaning is not tenable, because the ritual procedure for receiving the precepts does not involve discourse on principle.

If one says it is the stage of phenomena, there are two possibilities: either [the precepts] coexist with the substance of the mind, or they coexist with the physical form. Furthermore, [the precepts] must be conferred by ten masters upon a single person in the future.

The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) and the three aggregates (*triskandha*) are mutually contradictory dharmas; how, then, can they be identical? If one asks this, [the answer is:
according to the *Yuan ti zi chi ji*, it is said that [this practice] was adopted to support one's own school, and thus we know that it also existed within our own school.
Answer: The essence is one; this is discussed from two perspectives: first, regarding the opening and resolving [of the precepts], and second, regarding the non-equality [of the precepts].

This refers to the essence of the mind itself. Regarding the seventh point, the difficulty concerning the contradiction between the following and the observing: it is argued that the practice of maintaining and guarding [the precepts] must necessarily rely on the essence of the receiving [of the precepts].

It is not yet clear upon which essence one is currently relying to practice and guard them. If one says that both are guarded—just as when burning the body, arms, or fingers, or when grasping and keeping both [a human and an animal]—then [the distinction between the two cases would collapse].

If one attains merit through the Mahāyāna while committing offenses through the Hīnayāna, or incurs sin by selling alcohol or disparaging Bodhisattvas, yet the offenses of a Śrāvaka are considered light—how can such a vast discrepancy of a thousandfold differences in the gravity of upholding and violating precepts be reconciled so that both sides avoid fault?

If it is argued that one merely relies on the Hīnayāna, since the perfect essence has already been awakened, would it not be contradictory to the essence if one does not maintain and protect it? If...
To violate the essence [of one's own Vinaya] while relying on the practices of another is the fault of receiving [a precept] that contradicts its characteristics;
for example, Yijing received the essence of the Dharmaguptaka school but followed the practices of the Mūlasarvāstivāda.
Answer: Although the vow is generated within the perfect essence and its accompanying practices, one provisionally relies on the Hīnayāna;

yet, once the three clusters of precepts have been received, one should subsequently rely on the Mahāyāna for meditative concentration, and for the protection of conduct, one should follow the Mahāyāna practices.
This is extremely clear from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which prescribes various additional precepts beyond those of the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the objection concerning the contradiction between the eight categories of offenses (*aṣṭa-saṃghāvaśeṣa*) and the *Vibhaṅga*: it is argued that in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), even a momentary transgression and a grave condition have distinct boundaries and must not be confused.

If one were to establish offenses based on grave conditions, it would contradict the Perfect Teaching; yet if one were to establish them based on momentary transgressions, then for later students, the Vinaya would become useless. Why?
Because nothing is more essential within the Vinaya than the principles of observance and violation (*dhāraṇa* and *aticāra*). Now, since [the distinction is lost]...
"Why should one trouble oneself to study this?
The answer is: It is only after receiving the Bodhisattva precepts that one should then focus on even a momentary lapse to form the bond [of restraint].
Since the characteristics of both upholding and violating the precepts are entirely as described in the Vinaya, the intent of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding this matter is very clear.

9. The Objection Concerning the Contradiction in the Manner of Confessing Sins: The objection states: When confessing sins, if one simply performs a Mahāyāna confession, can the offense of violating the precepts be extinguished?
If you say it can, it is because the Patriarchs did not permit this, and thus they established the ritual for confessing the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍ-varga*).
If you say it cannot, then since the nature [of the offense] is Mahāyāna, would the sin not also be extinguished by relying on a Mahāyāna confession? For what reason is this so?
Furthermore, one may also generate the Mahāyāna mind and perform the sixfold repentance (*ṣaḍ-varga-pratikramaṇa*) to extinguish the paths of karma.

If it is argued that even the Patriarchs did not permit this, we respond that they established the Three Contemplations (*tri-darśana*) for this very reason. If it is argued that the karma is not extinguished, this would contradict your own established doctrine;

for when they receive the precepts, it is said they "generate the Mahāyāna mind," and thus upon the altar they immediately give rise to the Perfect Body (*pariniṣpanna-kāya*). This is the method of repentance.

One should also apply this analogy by saying that because one has resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind, the transgressions of the precepts are extinguished through repentance; why then do you say they are not extinguished?
Furthermore, for what reason is one [method] perfect while the other is not?

Answer: Although the essence [of the offense] may be encompassed by universal repentance, one must nevertheless perform specific karmic practices. Even the Mahayana ritual repentance explained in the *Shu* (Commentary) cannot extinguish karma;
how much less can the minor repentance used after having aroused the great mind extinguish the paths of karma?

The Tenth Difficulty: The Challenge Regarding the Lack of Scriptural Basis for the Arising [of the Perfect Body]. The challenge states: As for the claim that "one who receives the Small Vehicle dharma immediately gives rise to the essence of the Perfect [Vehicle]," on what basis is this established?

For instance, in the *Śīla-sūtra* (Shan jie jing), it says that in order to obtain the subsequent Bodhisattva precepts, one first gives rise to the Mahāyāna mind and takes the fiftyfold set of precepts as a preparatory means (*upāya*).
Nowhere does it say that receiving the fiftyfold set of precepts itself gives rise to the Perfect [Vehicle].

Because it is the essence, the Patriarchs also followed the sutras and precepts, stating that one must rely upon the seven groups of precepts as a preliminary expedient (*pūrvaprayoga*) in order to obtain the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*).
Some say this is for the sake of fulfilling the three clusters of pure precepts (*triskandha-śīla*), while others say the intent lies in what follows;

yet they do not explicitly state that receiving the minor precepts is itself [the Great Precepts]. If one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (Duolun), those who aspire to the superior grade of resolve...
This interpretation is not correct; those are merely the Bodhisattva precepts shared within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) for those of the Two Vehicles.

Alternatively, it may be that one should take the minor precepts of the superior-grade resolve as a skillful means (*upāya*) for the subsequent Bodhisattva precepts. Why then do you claim they are directly [the ultimate] themselves?

If you say they refer to that [ultimate level], then even within the various Vinaya sections of the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanzong*), it is taught that there is the arousal of the resolve for the Three Vehicles.

The mind, too, ought to be circular; if that were so, it would not only be a matter of the inversion of large and small, but also a case where the meaning applies universally across all four divisions—why then [is it otherwise]?

If one points to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* or the *Mahā-śāstra*, this is also incorrect, for those texts merely explain the manifestation of the Mahāyāna as something to be studied extensively, but do not describe the ritual procedures for receiving the precepts of either the Mahāyāna or the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, the Patriarch also cited the *Dharma-*... [text truncated]

The statement in the *Huayan* [Sutra] that "in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle" indicates, by way of revelation and manifestation, the destination to which practitioners return;
how could it ever be intended here to immediately establish the essence? There are textual authorities among these various meanings that clarify the Master’s intent.
The *Ābhāṣa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "The precepts of all ordinary beings and sages alike take the mind as their essence. Now, based on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, this mind is analyzed and resolved;
since it is vast, its essence is consequently vast. As for the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and others, they are all subsumed under this principle;
the meaning may be seen in the commentary.
The inquiry regarding the basis of the fourth, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), asks: Upon which sutras and treatises is this Perfect Teaching said to rely?

If it is claimed that it is established based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* through the process of revelation (*kaixian*), then one must investigate the Perfect Teaching in relation to the three schools of thought concerning the essence of the precepts (*jie-ti*), which are correctly derived from the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). Upon searching for that Perfect Teaching therein:
In the preceding and following passages of this chapter, there is no mention at all of establishing [the teaching] based on the *opening and revealing* (kai-xian);

it is only upon reaching the section on "general attribution" that the *Lotus Sūtra* is cited, so we now know where its ultimate destination lies. How can you claim that this serves as the basis for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao)?
If you say it is based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this would be a great confusion of the gates of the Dharma. Why? Because the Tathāgata’s teachings possess a great [distinction].
There is the "Small" (Hīnayāna), the "Regulation" (Vinaya), and the "Transformation" (Upadeśa). The Vinaya constitutes the Regulation; the Sūtras and Śāstras constitute the Transformation.
The Tripiṭaka is the Small, while the Mahāyāna is the Great Vehicle. Now, let us ask: Is the present *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* a Regulation, a Transformation, Great, or Small?
If one says it is neither Transformation nor Great, but is Regulation and Small, then the teachings of the Regulation merely clarify [the precepts].

If one holds that the phenomena of the *śīla* (precepts) and transgressions pertain only to the Small Vehicle and do not extend to the discourse of the Perfect Vehicle (*yāna*), then where does the *Caturvargika-vinaya* establish the meaning of "perfection"?

Furthermore, in what passage within the single system of the *Caturvargika-vinaya* is the name and meaning of the "Perfect Teaching" (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) or "Consciousness-Only" (*vijñaptimātra*) taught?
If it is argued that these five meanings are "partially applicable" (*prabheda-sāmānya*), this is not so; for they are precisely what should be understood as the "partially applicable" [teachings].

From the perspective of principle, if that [the *dharmadhātu*] is taken as the essence of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), why would it be necessary to further establish a separate essence for the School of Emptiness (*kongzong*)?

Therefore, upon examining the "Chapter on the Perfect Teaching" (*Yuanzong Zhang*), one does not see anywhere that it establishes the essence of the Perfect Teaching based on the *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü*). Thus, when correctly setting forth its essence, it says:
"It forms seeds of goodness within the fundamental storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). From what source, then, is the name and meaning of this "storehouse consciousness" derived?
If that is so, upon what sutras and treatises does Ye-jie-er-bi (Yaśomitra) base his establishment of the name and meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)?

Answer: It is divided into the "present" and the "past. The "present perfect" refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which supports the rules (*vinaya*) and discusses the eternal (*chang*), ultimately manifesting the nature (*xing*).

The "past perfect" refers to the second intention of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the opening and manifestation—as well as the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra* and others. In the context of the past perfect, [the present perfect] serves as a secondary supplement.

Now, as for the Perfect [Teaching], it is the Correct; though the Correct is divided into the Present and the Past, there is no difference between them. This is fully evident in the text on the "Perfect Precept-essence.
I ask you to please read it.
Fifth: Doubts regarding the Three Contemplations in One Mind.

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as entered through Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), is it a simultaneous, holistic contemplation (*yuan-guan*) or a sequential contemplation (*ci-di-guan*)? If one says it is a sequential contemplation, since the contemplation of Consciousness-Only is practiced by those of perfect realization (*yuan-ren*), how could it be a partial, sequential contemplation? Therefore, in the *Guijing yi* (Ritual of Homage), it is sometimes said: "Following their initial step, they must rely on two conditions," or it is said: [The text continues: "Furthermore, the contemplation of the three natures is not merely a sequential practice; rather, it is a simultaneous contemplation that encompasses all three natures at once. This is because the three natures are mutually inclusive within the single mind. When contemplating the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one simultaneously contemplates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Likewise, when contemplating the dependent nature, one simultaneously contemplates the other two.

Thus, although the gates of entry may differ—whether entering through the imagined nature, the dependent nature, or the perfected nature—the ultimate realization is that all three natures are perfectly interfused within the single mind of Consciousness-Only. This is why the *Guijing yi* states that one must rely on two conditions: the condition of the object (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the condition of the dominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*). By relying on these two conditions, one realizes that the three natures are non-dual and identical within the single reality of Consciousness-Only. Therefore, while there are distinctions in the gates of entry, the contemplation itself is fundamentally a simultaneous, holistic realization.

Whether it be said that the initial and final minds are equal, or that one contemplates both the ultimate and the conventional simultaneously, or as the *Yuecheng yeshu* states that one contemplates this within the contemplation—how could these various texts not refer to the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*) of the beginner?
If one were to say that this is the perfect contemplation of a single mind, it would greatly contradict the present treatise. Why is this?

Because in that text, the characteristics of the cultivation of the four stages of consciousness-only are each distinct; the semblance and the ultimate are not the same, for at first, one begins with the semblance.

One enters the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) by means of phenomena resembling objects; next, one enters the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*) through the four types of investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*);

and finally, one enters the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) through ultimate wisdom. Only then does one enter the stages (*bhūmi*) based on the object and realize the truth; prior to this, the first two contemplations are naturally complete.
Thus, it is known that the sequence of the three contemplations in this fundamental treatise lacks entirely the sense of a beginner practicing them in a perfected, simultaneous manner.

If it is said that the Patriarch’s establishment of this doctrine might lose its original intent, Nanshan himself cites the four stages of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as being accessible to both ordinary beings and sages alike;
yet, while others raise objections despite this accessibility, they truly do not understand what these are.

For within the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* itself there are three types: emptiness, existence, and the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Others object that *vijñapti-mātra* is identical to the Middle Way.

The teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) does not mean that what ordinary beings cultivate through their aspirations and inclinations is the same as the *vijñapti-mātra* of emptiness and existence; although the names are identical, their essences are not one.

Since the *vijñapti-mātra* of emptiness and existence fundamentally refutes [the views of] those prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), what is there to be surprised about regarding the cultivation during the stage of aspiration (*adhimukti-avasthā*)?
We respectfully request a clear resolution so that the textual meaning may be consistent throughout.
Answer: Regarding the application of contemplation, it is a single mind of perfect observation; regarding the realization of severance and proof, it follows the sequence of the three natures.
As for the question concerning the sixth consciousness of *vijñaptimātra* as it pertains to the four stages:

if one says it pertains to all four stages, then once the cognition of the rope has ceased and one enters true observation (*tattvadarśana*), it would only pertain to the realization of the ultimate truth.
Regarding the object as it truly is, because it does not arise when the wisdom of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) ceases, the treatise asks:
"Does 'consciousness-only' refer to the subject that observes, or to the object that is observed?

The answer is: Consciousness-only actually pervades all four stages; although the wisdom of the rope may cease, the wisdom of the hemp remains. Please observe this in the "Homage and Dedication" section.
Regarding the response of Kongfang Xian and the text of Vasubandhu’s *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is further asked:
"Is consciousness-only the subject that observes (*ālambaka*) or the object that is observed (*ālambana*?

The answer is: In the preceding passage, the treatise cites the text stating that "the semblance of phenomena and their meanings, as well as names and meanings, are mutually [identical]"; for what reason do you still remain confused about the relationship between subject and object?

Yes. Regarding the seventh point, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* clarifies that in cultivating the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one employs non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). As for the characteristics of this wisdom itself—
There are five kinds [of separation]: first, separation from non-reflection; second, separation from the stage of non-investigation and non-analysis (*avitarka-avicāra*);

third, separation from the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*); fourth, separation from the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*); and fifth, separation from divergent conceptualization regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*).
It is not yet clear how these five meanings are ultimately separated.
Answer: Because it is precisely in its separation from these five meanings that it is named "non-conceptual wisdom" (nirvikalpa-jñāna), the Commentary states:

"That which is separated from the five aspects, which takes the true meaning as its object and proceeds toward the true meaning. Furthermore, the Great Master said: "It is that which manifests by accumulating emptiness."
Regarding the eighth characteristic, the emptiness of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa-śūnyatā*):
one may inquire whether the contemplation of the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of conceptual differentiation are identical or distinct.

If they are said to be identical, then the emptiness of characteristics is that practiced by small bodhisattvas during stages such as the "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*), whereas the emptiness of conceptual differentiation is the entry into the stage of faith (*adhimukti*) by great bodhisattvas, which is the consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) perspective.
Regarding the cultivation of the stages and so forth, how could these distinct gates—differentiated by faculties and categorized as Great or Small—possibly be conflated?
If they were identical, why would it be necessary to laboriously establish the "contemplation of the emptiness of characteristics" as a separate stage?

Furthermore, within the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) system, if one establishes "expedient emptiness" as a distinct stage, why not also establish "dependent origination" (*paratantra*) as a distinct stage? If you say...
Is it because the names and meanings of the two types of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are not different that Vasubandhu’s commentary reconciles them?
Answer: The three contemplations encompass emptiness, and non-emptiness likewise encompasses non-existence; is this not a case where the names differ but the meaning is the same?

If one were to distinguish between emptiness and the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), according to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*’s analysis of the three doubts and four differences, it would be the same as the emptiness of characteristics.
The discrepancy between what was stated previously and what follows should be examined by consulting the "Chapter on the Emptiness of Characteristics" (*Lakṣaṇaśūnyatā-parivarta*).
Ninth, regarding the question of how the founder of the Nanshan school’s established tenets (*siddhānta*) deviate from his master:

since the founder of the Nanshan school was a direct successor to the Primordial Master, yet the Primordial Master established causality as his tenet, while the founder of the Nanshan school [proceeded] directly... [text fragment].

Taking the precepts as the fundamental tenet (as recorded in Master Yang’s *Yi-tu*, which summarizes the differing tenets established by nine schools). If this is so, does this not contradict the relationship between teacher and disciple?

If one establishes a tenet that runs counter to what was received from a master, where does the principle of "receiving and following" reside? Furthermore, what profound intention lies behind Nanshan’s deviation from his master?
Answer: If one establishes the Southern School based on taking refuge and paying homage, it does not necessarily take the precepts alone as its primary tenet;
yet, even if it ultimately takes the precepts as its primary tenet, how could there ever be the fault of contradicting the Master?

As is clearly seen in the differing ways that Xianshou, Qingliang, and Guifeng established their teachings and categorized the texts, how could this hinder those who receive and uphold the transmission? Since such cases have been numerous throughout the ages, why should one trouble oneself over them?
Doubt. Regarding the tenth fascicle of the *Shiyi*, the "Ten Gates" (*Shimen*) which are subsumed under various sections, the *Yiwen Chao* states:
"These ten articles all collectively belong to the various gates; if the first [gate] establishes the fundamental principle and manifests the virtues..."
In the subsequent sections on the miscellaneous practices of the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha and so forth, the characteristics of the ten gates shall be distinguished;
their specific features will be demonstrated in detail within the three chapters concerning the beginning, middle, and end, while the remaining cases shall be understood by analogy.
Answer: These ten sections merely provide a general summary of the main intent of the *Tongshu*; among its various chapters, some are complete while others are missing.
How can one treat them all with the same brush? I hope you will reconsider this further; it should not be decided so hastily.
